title: SYSK Distraction Playlist: How Rodney Dangerfield Worked, Live From LA
summary: Live recording at the LA Podcast Festival (rebroadcast as a distraction playlist episode) in which Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant profile comedian Rodney Dangerfield. They cover his neglected childhood under his vaudevillian father's absence and his mother's coldness, his teen joke-writing and early work as a singing waiter and diver, his 1970s comeback under the Rodney Dangerfield name (borrowed from a Jack Benny character), his Ed Sullivan and Johnny Carson breakthroughs, his Manhattan club Dangerfield's, his films (Caddyshack, Easy Money, Back to School, Natural Born Killers), his Grammy for No Respect, his lawsuit against Star magazine, his final Howard Stern interview and death after surgery, his funeral, and his rejected Academy membership. Includes a sponsor read, a mid-show ad break, and a joke-telling segment.
topics: Jack Benny character origin of stage name
Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences membership rejection
Stuff You Should Know live episode

segments.title: Live show opening and banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the live LA Podcast Festival recording with banter, audience greetings, and a plug for sponsors Audible and Squarespace, then introduce the Rodney Dangerfield topic.

segments.title: No respect and inner pain
segments.summary: The hosts introduce Dangerfield's 'no respect' persona, an anecdote about a fan asking for butter, and how comedians' inner pain drove his material. They describe his persistent heaviness and sadness offstage.

segments.title: Childhood neglect and early hustle
segments.summary: Dangerfield was born Jacob Cohen on Long Island; his vaudevillian father left, and his mother was emotionally absent. He raised himself from about age eight, delivered groceries to classmates, and recounts being exploited by local molesters for money as a child.

segments.title: Writing jokes and early career
segments.summary: Dangerfield began writing jokes around age fifteen and sold them to comics, keeping them in a stuffed bag. At nineteen he got a resort job in the Catskills, sang as a waiter and worked as a diver, then married Joyce Indig in 1951, moved to New Jersey, and quit comedy at 27.

segments.title: Comeback and the Rodney Dangerfield name
segments.summary: At about 41 Dangerfield returned to comedy and developed a persona. The club booker picked the name Rodney Dangerfield, taken from a Jack Benny character; Benny later praised him. His Ed Sullivan appearance led to many late-night spots including Carson.

segments.title: Dangerfield's club and mentoring young comics
segments.summary: Dangerfield borrowed about a million dollars to open his own New York comedy club, Dangerfield's, to be home with his children. It succeeded, and the club's HBO specials launched careers including Seinfeld, Chris Rock, and Jim Carrey.

segments.title: Film career and Caddyshack
segments.summary: Dangerfield appeared in Kubrick's The Killing and The Projectionist, then in Caddyshack, where he was allowed to do his act on camera. He disliked the film process, comparing it to live performance. Critic Ben Fong-Torres's description of his onstage persona is read aloud.

segments.title: Sponsor break for podcast event
segments.summary: Mid-show ad break promoting The Message, a podcast from Panoply and the GE Podcast Theater.

segments.title: Easy Money, Back to School, and later career
segments.summary: Dangerfield wrote and starred in Easy Money, reviewed by Roger Ebert. Back to School became a major hit in 1986. He won a Grammy for No Respect, and the Smithsonian received his red tie and shirt. He appeared in Miller Lite commercials and released the rap single Rapping Rodney. He was on The Simpsons as Mr. Burns' ... (hosts' Simpsons reference), and wrote a romance novel.

segments.title: Lawsuit against Star magazine
segments.summary: Dangerfield sued Star magazine for libel over claims about his drinking and drug use. The court awarded him damages, and his later attempt to pursue the parent company reached the Supreme Court, per the hosts.

segments.title: Final Howard Stern interview, death, and funeral
segments.summary: In his last Howard Stern interview he discussed his childhood and his upcoming surgery; he fell into a coma, had a heart attack, and died. His funeral included pallbearers such as Jim Carrey, Chris Rock, and Adam Sandler, and Michael Bolton was too emotional to sing. The hosts also mention a Scout role he was never in.

segments.title: Academy rejection and Rodney.com
segments.summary: The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences rejected his membership, with a letter from Roddy McDowall. Dangerfield built one of the first entertainment websites, and the Academy later invited him, but he declined. The hosts note his website still exists.

segments.title: Closing jokes and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts trade Dangerfield jokes, invite listeners to get in touch by Twitter, Facebook, and email, and sign off.
